passage:
The following text is adapted from Frederick Douglass's 1852 speech “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?”

Fellow-citizens, pardon me, allow me to ask, why am I called upon to speak here to-day? What have I, or those I represent, to do with your national independence? Are the great principles of political freedom and of natural justice, embodied in that Declaration of Independence, extended to us?
stem: Which choice best describes the function of the questions in the text?
choices: They challenge the audience to recognize that the freedoms being celebrated are denied to enslaved people.
They ask the audience for factual information about the history of the Declaration of Independence.
They express Douglass's uncertainty about whether he was correctly invited to give the speech.
They introduce a lighthearted tone before Douglass turns to more serious matters later on.
steps: The questions are rhetorical: Douglass knows the answers.
Asking whether the Declaration's principles are “extended to us” points out that they are not, for enslaved people.
He isn't seeking facts, isn't really unsure about his invitation, and the tone isn't lighthearted.
key: Rhetorical questions make a point; decide what point the speaker expects listeners to see.
